141.title: Flowers that fade
141.hook: a traditional offering verse: these flowers fade, and so will this body
141.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists offer fresh flowers at shrines and temples while chanting a short Pali verse that reflects that, as the flowers wither, so will the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, buddharupa, a Buddha on the shelf: kept high and clean, pointing past itself, with customs that differ by country. Your line was customs differ, care doesn't.

Roses on an anniversary. A bouquet at a wedding. Plastic flowers, even, so they never droop. Gift flowers tend to say forever. The freshest ones get picked, and when they start to brown they go out with the trash, quickly, a little embarrassed, as if the flowers had failed. Buddhist temples are full of flowers too: jasmine, lotus, frangipani, marigolds, heaped in front of the Buddha. But there's a verse people chant while offering them, and it says something you'd never write on a card.
screen: `ROSES THAT SAY FOREVER.` → `OUT THEY GO, EMBARRASSED.` → `A VERSE YOU'D NEVER WRITE ON A CARD.`

segments.voice: The Theravada flower offering is a short Pali chant. It begins with the flowers themselves: full of color, full of fragrance, offered at the feet of the Buddha. Then it turns. In substance it says: just as these flowers will wither, so my body will go to destruction. Try saying that while holding a fresh bunch of jasmine. It's not meant to be gloomy, though. It's honest. The flowers are chosen precisely because they're fresh, and precisely because they won't last. That's anicca, impermanence: everything that arises passes away. The flower shows it in a few days; the body, over a lifetime. The Dhammapada uses flowers the same way. In Max Muller's translation: "Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers, and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village." Someone so busy picking pleasures they don't notice the water rising. The offering reverses that. You pick a flower, and you notice. What does noticing do? Some teachers say it makes things more precious, not less. Jasmine that will be brown by Thursday is worth smelling today. A face across the dinner table, remembered as not forever, can be looked at a little longer. So the verse isn't asking you to be sad about fading. It's asking you to be awake while the flower is fresh. Buddhists offer flowers as respect for the Buddha, and as a mirror. The flowers are fresh today. That is exactly why they're beautiful.
screen: `COLOR, FRAGRANCE, AT HIS FEET.` · `AS THESE FADE, SO WILL THIS BODY.` · `ANICCA: EVERYTHING PASSES.` · `THE FLOOD AND THE SLEEPING VILLAGE.` · then, large: `FRESH TODAY, GONE TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: If you have a flower, a leaf, or even a picture of one, set it in front of you and look closely for a few breaths: the color, the edges, where it's already starting to change. Then feel your own hands, warm, alive, also changing. Let each breath come and go, arising and passing, fresh and then gone; there's nothing to fix.
Puppha. Flower: the offering verse, as these flowers will wither, so will this body, and so this moment is worth waking up for.
Your line: fresh today, gone tomorrow. A flower can fade in its own time. Until tomorrow.

142.title: Candle and incense
142.hook: light for wisdom, scent for good conduct spreading
142.howItsDone: Buddhists offer candles or oil lamps and incense at shrines and temples, often with short Pali chants; the light is linked to dispelling darkness, and the texts link fragrance to virtue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, puppha, flowers that fade: as these flowers wither, so will this body. Your line was fresh today, gone tomorrow.

Sandalwood. Jasmine. Something smoky and sweet that stays in your clothes all afternoon. In a Buddhist temple, the nose often gets there before the eyes. Then the eyes adjust: dozens of small flames, candles and oil lamps flickering in front of a golden figure. Light and scent. They're easy to take for decoration, like candles on a restaurant table. But in the chants and texts behind them, each one stands for something specific. And the scent comes with a riddle the Buddha's attendant once asked him: is there a fragrance that can travel against the wind?
screen: `SANDALWOOD IN YOUR CLOTHES.` → `DOZENS OF SMALL FLAMES.` → `A SCENT AGAINST THE WIND?`

segments.voice: Start with the light. In the Theravada candle offering, people offer light to the Buddha, whom the chant calls the light of the three worlds, the one who dispels darkness. A candle is an easy picture of wisdom: where it's lit, you can see what's actually there. Darkness in the tradition often stands for avijja, ignorance, not seeing things as they are. Lighting a candle is a small wish to see clearly. Now the scent. Incense is offered too, and the texts give fragrance a meaning of its own. Here's the riddle. In a short discourse, Ananda asks the Buddha: the scents of roots, of wood, of flowers all travel only with the wind. Is there any scent that goes with the wind, against the wind, and both ways? The Buddha says yes. When a person keeps the precepts, lives kindly and gives generously, their good name spreads in every direction, with the wind and against it. The Dhammapada puts it in a verse. In Max Muller's translation: "the odour of good people travels even against the wind; a good man pervades every place." So incense is a picture of conduct. You don't see it spreading, but you smell it in every corner of the room. Good conduct works the same way: people notice it long after you've left. Light for wisdom; scent for virtue. Two strands of the path, seeing clearly and living well, offered as a flame and a thread of smoke.
screen: `LIGHT: THE ONE WHO DISPELS DARKNESS.` · `AVIJJA: NOT SEEING CLEARLY.` · `ANANDA'S RIDDLE OF THE WIND.` · `VIRTUE TRAVELS AGAINST THE WIND.` · then, large: `LIGHT AND SCENT.`

segments.voice: If you can do it safely, light a candle and set it somewhere steady, or simply picture one, and let your eyes rest softly on the flame, lighting the space around it without trying. Close your eyes and sense its glow, then bring to mind one person whose goodness you've felt, like a scent that stayed in the room, and let the breath carry that. When you finish, blow the candle out.
Candle and incense. Light for wisdom, seeing clearly; scent for good conduct, which spreads even against the wind.
Your line: light and scent. Goodness spreads, even against the wind. Day one hundred forty-two, done.

143.title: Sharing the merit
143.hook: ending practice by dedicating whatever good was done to all beings
143.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions end ceremonies and meditation by dedicating the merit to others; in Theravada countries this is often done by pouring water while monks chant, and in Mahayana traditions with a dedication to the awakening of all beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, candle and incense: light for wisdom, scent for good conduct that travels against the wind. Your line was light and scent.

At the end of a Buddhist ceremony in Thailand, something small happens that visitors often miss. While the monks chant, people pour water from a little vessel into a bowl, a thin, steady stream, until the chant ends. Some hold a finger under the stream. Afterward, the water is often poured out at the foot of a tree. It looks like cleaning up. It isn't. It's the last and, many Buddhists would say, one of the most beautiful parts of practice: giving away the good you've just done.
screen: `A THIN STREAM OF WATER.` → `POURED AT THE FOOT OF A TREE.` → `GIVING AWAY THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is punna, usually translated merit: the goodness that comes from good actions, like giving, keeping the precepts, meditating. You'd think the natural thing is to keep it. But Buddhists across traditions end practice by sharing it. In Theravada this is called pattidana, the giving of merit. Its oldest roots are in a short text, the discourse outside the walls. It pictures dead relatives waiting outside the walls of their old home, hoping someone will remember them. When the living give food to monks and dedicate the gift, the text says the relatives can rejoice in it and be helped. The line people still chant is idam vo natinam hotu: may this be for our relatives. That's what the water pouring is, and many chants that go with it compare the merit to rivers filling the ocean. Someone who hears of your good deed and says sadhu, well done, shares it too, by rejoicing. In Mahayana traditions the dedication goes wider: at the end of a sitting or a chant, practitioners dedicate the merit to the awakening of all beings, everywhere, without exception. Yesterday's candle comes back here, because teachers often explain the logic with one. Light another candle from yours, and your flame doesn't get smaller. The room just gets brighter. Merit shared isn't merit lost. It quietly changes the one who shares, too. Ending with a dedication keeps practice from becoming a private savings account. You sat, you gave, you kept a precept, and then you open your hands again.
screen: `PUNNA: THE GOOD FROM GOOD ACTIONS.` · `RELATIVES OUTSIDE THE WALLS.` · `DEDICATED TO ALL BEINGS.` · `ONE CANDLE LIGHTS ANOTHER.` · then, large: `MAY IT BE SHARED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind whatever good came from this practice, a little calm, a little kindness, a little clarity, and picture it as water in a small cup. Pour it out in a thin, steady stream, flowing on to someone you love, someone you've lost, a stranger, all beings. If you'd like, use the old words, idam vo natinam hotu, may this be for our relatives; or simply open your hands.
Punna. Merit, the goodness from good actions: shared at the end of practice, like water poured out until it reaches the sea.
Your line: may it be shared. The good doesn't stop at you. See you tomorrow.

144.title: Your morning
144.howItsDone: Some Buddhists begin the day at a home shrine with bows, the homage chant, the refuges and precepts, a short sitting, loving-kindness and a dedication of merit, often closing with 'sadhu' three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, punna, sharing the merit: one candle lighting another, the good of practice given away. Your line was may it be shared. Today is the last day of the chant and the shrine.

How does your morning start now? On plenty of mornings it goes like this: an alarm, a thumb on a screen, the news, a group chat, somebody else's emergency, all before feet touch the floor. On a morning like that, the first ten minutes belong to whoever reached the phone first. This week you've collected the pieces of something else: not a new obligation, a different first ten minutes, built from parts you already know. Today i put them together, in order, and hand them to you.
screen: `AN ALARM, A THUMB, A SCREEN.` → `WHO OWNS THE FIRST TEN MINUTES?` → `PARTS YOU ALREADY KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's a shape built from those parts, close to what some Buddhists do at home, with many variations. One: the bow. At your quiet corner, or just beside the bed, three bows: Buddha, dhamma, sangha. Pride set down before the day picks it up. Two: homage. Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa, three times, turning the mind in one direction. Some people add the three refuges and the five precepts here, taking them fresh each day. If you'd like, light the candle, offer a flower. Three: the breath. Sit, and let the breath be known, long as long, short as short, the way you learned in the breathing weeks. Five minutes is plenty. Four: metta. The four phrases: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease. Start with yourself, then widen, to someone you'll see today, to everyone. Five: dedication. Whatever good came from these minutes, may it be shared. Then one word, said three times: sadhu, sadhu, sadhu. Good, well done. People say it at the end of a chant, a talk, a gift. It means: I rejoice in this. Look back and the whole week is here: the homage, the quiet corner, a Buddha on the shelf, flowers that fade, light and scent, the shared merit, now in order. Ten minutes. Nothing about it requires you to be calm first, or to feel spiritual. The shape is there on the mornings when nothing in you feels like it.
screen: `ONE: THE BOW. TWO: HOMAGE.` · `THREE: THE BREATH.` · `FOUR: METTA. FIVE: DEDICATION.` · `SADHU, SADHU, SADHU.` · then, large: `A MORNING, YOURS.`

segments.voice: Lower your head once, gently, and turn the mind toward what you value. Let the breath come and go and simply know it; then, may I be safe, may I be at ease, may everyone I meet today be at ease. Whatever good came from this, may it be shared, and if you like, say sadhu, quietly, three times.
Your morning. Bow, homage, breath, metta, dedication: ten minutes that belong to you before the day begins.
Your line: a morning, yours. Ten minutes, before anyone else gets them. Day one hundred forty-four, done.

145.title: Vesak
145.hook: the May full moon: in Theravada lands, birth, awakening and passing remembered on one day
145.howItsDone: On Vesak, Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing: many dress in white, visit temples, keep extra precepts, give food and light lanterns and lamps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your morning: bow, homage, breath, metta, dedication, and sadhu three times. Your line was a morning, yours. Now a new week: the holy days.

A birthday, a graduation and a funeral, all on the same day. Every year. With lanterns. That's roughly what the full moon of May holds across Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos, and in Buddhist communities worldwide. Streets fill with lights. Temples fill up. People dressed in white carry flowers and candles. It's a great holy day in these countries, and it holds three moments of one life at once.
screen: `A BIRTHDAY, A GRADUATION, A FUNERAL.` → `ALL ON ONE FULL MOON.` → `THREE MOMENTS OF ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Vesak. The name comes from Vesakha, the month in the old Indian calendar that usually falls in April or May. In Theravada tradition, three events in the Buddha's life are remembered on its full moon. His birth, in the garden at Lumbini. His awakening, under the tree at Bodh Gaya. And his passing into final nibbana, at Kusinara, eighty years later. Born, awake, gone: one life, one night. The awakening is remembered with a Dhammapada verse tradition places on the Buddha's lips that night, addressed to craving as the builder of the house of the self. In Max Muller's translation: "But now, maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again." His passing is remembered with his last words, from the long discourse on the final nibbana. In T. W. Rhys Davids' translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" So one night holds a baby's first breath and an old man's last. Tradition doesn't treat that as an accident of the calendar. It reads like the teaching itself: things arise, things pass, and in between, a person can wake up. In 1950 the World Fellowship of Buddhists, a gathering from many countries, agreed to keep Vesak together, and in 1999 the United Nations recognized it too. Other Buddhist traditions keep these events on separate days; you'll meet one tomorrow. Because it follows the moon, the date moves: some years it falls in June. And the lamp people light that night isn't for one moment. It's for the whole life.
screen: `VESAKHA: THE APRIL-MAY MOON.` · `BORN AT LUMBINI.` · `AWAKE AT BODH GAYA.` · `GONE AT KUSINARA.` · then, large: `BORN, AWAKE, GONE.`

segments.voice: Hold three moments of one life in mind, slowly: a baby's first breath in a garden, a man under a tree at dawn seeing clearly, an old man lying between two trees saying, keep going, with care. Then feel your own breath; it began once, and it will end once. Right now, in between, it's here, so rest in this one.
Vesak. The full moon of Vesakha, when Theravada Buddhists remember the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing on one day.
Your line: born, awake, gone. A baby's first breath and an old man's last, on one full moon. That's day one hundred forty-five.

146.title: Bathing the baby Buddha
146.hook: in Japan and elsewhere in East Asia the birth is kept in April by pouring sweet tea over a small standing Buddha
146.howItsDone: In Japan on April 8, temples set up a small flower-covered hall with a standing baby Buddha, and visitors pour sweet hydrangea tea (amacha) over it with a ladle; bathing ceremonies are also held in Korea, China and Taiwan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vesak: in Theravada lands, the birth, the awakening and the passing, all on one full moon. Your line was born, awake, gone.

April the eighth, a temple courtyard in Kyoto. There's a tiny hall made of flowers, the size of a dollhouse. Inside, in a shallow basin, stands a bronze baby, maybe a foot tall, one finger pointing at the sky and the other at the ground. A line of children and grandparents waits with small wooden ladles. One by one, they scoop up something golden from the basin and pour it gently over the baby's head. It's tea. Sweet tea.
screen: `APRIL 8, A TEMPLE IN KYOTO.` → `A BRONZE BABY IN A HALL OF FLOWERS.` → `SWEET TEA, POURED BY LADLE.`

segments.voice: Hanamatsuri. Hana: flower. Matsuri: festival. The flower festival is Japan's name for the Buddha's birthday, kept on April the eighth; its older temple name, kanbutsu-e, means the gathering for bathing the Buddha. In Theravada lands, birth, awakening and passing share one day. In much of East Asia, the birth has its own day, in spring. Korea keeps it on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month, and China and Taiwan have a bathing ceremony too. The story behind the scene: tradition says the baby was born in a garden, at Lumbini, which is why the little hall is covered in flowers. As soon as he was born, it says, he stood, took seven steps, and pointed one hand up and one hand down, announcing that this was his last birth. And the old texts say water came down from the sky to bathe him. In the Pali discourse on wonderful qualities, two streams appear, one cool, one warm. In Chinese tellings it's nine dragons pouring from above. So people pour, too. The golden tea is amacha, a sweet tea made from a kind of hydrangea leaf, standing in for the water from the sky, or in some tellings, a rain of nectar. Why bathe a statue? Not because the Buddha needs cleaning. The gesture is welcome and wonder, like washing a newborn. Some teachers draw a second meaning: water poured over a newborn is a reminder that anyone can begin again. A clean beginning, as often as one is needed.

Then turn the picture toward yourself: something from this week you'd like to rinse off and start fresh. Don't argue with it; just picture the water running over it while the breath goes on.

147.title: Lanterns
147.hook: Vesak lanterns in Sri Lanka, lotus lanterns in Korea: light for the many
147.howItsDone: On the Buddha's day, Sri Lankan families hang handmade Vesak lanterns and cities build illuminated gateways, while in Korea temples hang lotus lanterns and Seoul holds the Yeondeunghoe lantern parade.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hanamatsuri, the flower festival: sweet tea poured over a small bronze baby. Your line was a clean beginning.

Two cities on the Buddha's day. In Colombo at dusk, every house seems to have hung something in the window or over the gate: paper lanterns in stars and octagons, bamboo frames covered in colored tissue, swaying in the warm air. In Seoul, a river of light pours down one of the city's big avenues: crowds carrying lanterns shaped like lotus flowers, dragons, elephants, the baby Buddha. Two countries, two different Buddhist traditions, the same instinct: make light, and put it where others can see it.
screen: `COLOMBO: A LANTERN AT EVERY GATE.` → `SEOUL: A RIVER OF LOTUS LIGHTS.` → `LIGHT WHERE OTHERS CAN SEE IT.`

segments.voice: In Sri Lanka, the Vesak lantern is called a kudu. Families often make their own from thin bamboo sticks and colored paper, and there are competitions for the most beautiful. Streets are also lined with huge lit gateways, called thoranas or pandals, painted with scenes from the Jataka stories you met in the stories camp, and blazing with colored bulbs. In Korea, the lantern festival is called Yeondeunghoe, the gathering for lighting lanterns. Its records reach back to the old Korean kingdoms, and in 2020 UNESCO recognized it as part of the world's living heritage. Temples hang rows of lotus lanterns across their courtyards, many with small paper tags carrying the names and wishes of the families who offered them. Why lanterns? You know part of the answer: two days ago, the lamp people light on Vesak; last week, light as a picture of wisdom; and before that, Nanda's lamp. But a lantern adds something a candle on a shrine doesn't. It's hung outside, over the gate, carried through the streets. The light is for whoever walks by: neighbors, strangers, people of every faith and none. Nobody asks who deserves to see it. That echoes a line in the old texts: the Buddha, they say, taught out of compassion for the world, for the good of the many. A lantern in the window is that idea made of paper and bamboo.

segments.voice: Picture a paper lantern, any shape you like, a lotus, a star, a simple box, glowing outside your front door or in your window. Let whoever passes tonight walk through its light: a neighbor, a delivery driver, a child on the way home. Wish each one well: may you be safe, may you be at ease.
Lanterns. Vesak lanterns in Sri Lanka, lotus lanterns in Korea: light hung where everyone passing can see it.
Your line: light for the many. A lantern in the window doesn't ask who's walking by. One hundred forty-seven days now.
